subject: political_science
chapter_title: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

concepts.title: The Split in the Congress (1969)
concepts.definition: The split in the Congress party in 1969 was a major political event in which the party divided into two factions -- the Congress (Organisation) led by the old guard (the Syndicate) and the Congress (Requisitionists) led by Indira Gandhi. The split arose from a power struggle between Indira Gandhi and the party's old leadership after the death of Lal Bahadur Shastri.
concepts.key_idea: The 1969 split had several causes and consequences: (1) after Shastri's death in 1966, Indira Gandhi became PM with the Syndicate's support, but tensions grew over policy; (2) the Syndicate backed the conservative candidate N. Sanjeeva Reddy for President in 1969, while Indira Gandhi supported V.V. Giri, who won; (3) the party formally split -- Indira's faction became Congress (R) and the old guard's became Congress (O); (4) Indira Gandhi adopted radical populist policies -- nationalisation of banks, abolition of privy purses -- to consolidate her position; (5) the split marked the end of the 'Congress system' of consensus politics.
question_patterns: What were the main causes of the split in the Congress party in 1969?
Explain the role of the Syndicate in the 1969 Congress split.
How did the presidential election of 1969 contribute to the Congress split?
Describe the consequences of the 1969 split in the Congress party.
How did Indira Gandhi consolidate her position after the 1969 split?

solution_steps.action: State the background of the split
solution_steps.explain: Note that after Shastri's death in 1966, Indira Gandhi became PM with the Syndicate's support, but tensions grew between her and the old guard over policy and power.

solution_steps.action: Explain the immediate cause
solution_steps.explain: Describe the 1969 presidential election, in which the Syndicate backed N. Sanjeeva Reddy while Indira Gandhi supported V.V. Giri, who won -- the trigger for the formal split.

solution_steps.action: Describe the consequences
solution_steps.explain: Explain that the party split into Congress (R) under Indira Gandhi and Congress (O) under the Syndicate, that Indira adopted radical populist policies (bank nationalisation, abolition of privy purses), and that this marked the end of the 'Congress system'.

worked_examples.question: What were the main causes of the split in the Congress party in 1969?
worked_examples.solution: The main causes of the 1969 split were: (1) a power struggle between Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and the old guard of the party, known as the Syndicate, after the death of Lal Bahadur Shastri in 1966; (2) ideological differences -- Indira Gandhi wanted a radical, left-leaning programme, while the Syndicate favoured a conservative, business-friendly approach; (3) the immediate trigger was the 1969 presidential election -- the Syndicate backed N. Sanjeeva Reddy, but Indira Gandhi supported the independent candidate V.V. Giri, who won. This defiance led to the formal split of the party into Congress (R) and Congress (O).
worked_examples.answer: Causes -- power struggle with the Syndicate, ideological differences, and the 1969 presidential election over Reddy vs Giri.

worked_examples.question: How did Indira Gandhi consolidate her position after the 1969 split?
worked_examples.solution: After the 1969 split, Indira Gandhi consolidated her position by adopting a radical populist programme. She (1) nationalised major banks in 1969; (2) abolished the privy purses and privileges of former princely rulers in 1970; (3) adopted the slogan 'Garibi Hatao' (Remove Poverty); (4) presented herself as the champion of the poor against the rich and the old guard; (5) called early elections in 1971 and won a massive mandate, legitimising her leadership and the split.
worked_examples.answer: Indira Gandhi consolidated power via bank nationalisation, abolition of privy purses, the 'Garibi Hatao' slogan, and a landslide in the 1971 elections.

concepts.title: The 1967 General Elections
concepts.definition: The 1967 general elections were the fourth Lok Sabha elections, held in the context of severe economic hardship, food shortages, inflation and popular discontent. The Congress party's dominance was significantly reduced -- it lost seats in the Lok Sabha and in several states, and non-Congress governments were formed in many states for the first time.
concepts.key_idea: Key features of the 1967 elections: (1) context -- droughts, food crisis, devaluation of the rupee (1966), inflation and price rise; (2) the Congress won a reduced majority in the Lok Sabha (283 seats) and lost power in eight states; (3) non-Congress coalitions (Samyukta Vidhayak Dal, SVD) formed governments in states like Bihar, UP, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab; (4) the elections marked the emergence of coalition politics at the state level; (5) it signalled the beginning of the decline of the 'Congress system' of one-party dominance.

solution_steps.action: Describe the context of the 1967 elections
solution_steps.explain: State that the elections were held amid severe economic hardship -- droughts, food shortages, the 1966 rupee devaluation, and inflation -- which created popular discontent.

solution_steps.action: Explain the results
solution_steps.explain: Note that the Congress won a reduced majority in the Lok Sabha (283 seats) and lost power in eight states, where non-Congress coalitions (SVD governments) were formed.

solution_steps.action: Explain the significance
solution_steps.explain: Describe how the elections marked the emergence of coalition politics at the state level and signalled the beginning of the decline of the 'Congress system' of one-party dominance.

worked_examples.question: What was the significance of the 1967 general elections in India?
worked_examples.solution: The 1967 general elections were significant because they marked the first major challenge to Congress dominance. The Congress party's majority in the Lok Sabha was sharply reduced, and it lost power in eight states. Non-Congress coalitions, called Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments, were formed in states like Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab. These elections marked the emergence of coalition politics at the state level and signalled the beginning of the decline of the 'Congress system' of one-party dominance that had prevailed since independence.
worked_examples.answer: 1967 elections -- reduced Congress majority, loss of power in eight states, rise of SVD coalitions, and the beginning of the decline of Congress dominance.

worked_examples.question: Explain the causes of the Congress party's poor performance in the 1967 elections.
worked_examples.solution: The Congress party's poor performance in 1967 was caused by: (1) severe economic hardship -- successive droughts in the mid-1960s led to food shortages and dependence on imported wheat; (2) high inflation and price rise that hurt ordinary people; (3) the devaluation of the rupee in 1966, which was unpopular; (4) growing discontent with the Congress's long rule and its perceived corruption and unresponsiveness; (5) the consolidation of opposition parties, which formed electoral alliances to defeat the Congress. Together these factors eroded the Congress's popular support.
worked_examples.answer: Causes -- food crisis, inflation, rupee devaluation, discontent with Congress rule, and opposition alliances.

concepts.title: Coalition Governments after 1967
concepts.definition: After the 1967 elections, non-Congress coalition governments -- known as Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments -- were formed in several Indian states. These coalitions brought together parties of diverse ideologies, from socialists and communists to the Jana Sangh and Swatantra Party, united mainly by their opposition to the Congress.
concepts.key_idea: Features of the post-1967 coalition governments: (1) they were formed in states like Bihar, UP, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab and West Bengal; (2) they united ideologically diverse parties -- socialists, communists, Jana Sangh, Swatantra and regional parties -- under the single aim of defeating the Congress; (3) they were often unstable due to ideological differences and factionalism; (4) many collapsed within a short period, leading to President's Rule; (5) despite instability, they demonstrated that non-Congress alternatives were possible and pioneered coalition politics in India.

solution_steps.action: Describe the formation of the SVD governments
solution_steps.explain: State that after the 1967 elections, non-Congress coalitions called Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments were formed in several states, uniting diverse opposition parties.

solution_steps.action: Explain their composition and instability
solution_steps.explain: Note that these coalitions brought together socialists, communists, the Jana Sangh, Swatantra and regional parties, and that they were often unstable due to ideological differences and factionalism, with many collapsing into President's Rule.

solution_steps.action: Explain their significance
solution_steps.explain: Describe how, despite their instability, the SVD governments demonstrated that non-Congress alternatives were possible and pioneered coalition politics in India.

worked_examples.question: What were the Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments? Explain their composition.
worked_examples.solution: The Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments were non-Congress coalition governments formed in several Indian states after the 1967 elections. Their composition was remarkable for its ideological diversity -- they brought together socialist parties, the Communist Party of India, the Jana Sangh (a right-wing Hindu nationalist party), the Swatantra Party (a pro-business conservative party) and various regional parties. For example, in Bihar, the SVD government included the Jana Sangh and the CPI. These parties were united not by a common ideology but by the single aim of keeping the Congress out of power.
worked_examples.answer: SVD governments = non-Congress state coalitions (1967) uniting socialists, communists, Jana Sangh, Swatantra and regional parties against the Congress.

worked_examples.question: Why were the post-1967 coalition governments unstable?
worked_examples.solution: The post-1967 coalition governments were unstable for several reasons: (1) ideological incompatibility -- the coalitions brought together parties ranging from communists to the right-wing Jana Sangh, with no common programme; (2) they were united only by anti-Congressism, which was a negative bond that could not sustain cooperation; (3) factionalism and personal ambitions of leaders led to defections; (4) the Congress, though weakened, actively worked to topple these governments and lure defectors; (5) many SVD governments collapsed within months, leading to President's Rule under Article 356. Their instability showed the limits of purely anti-Congress coalitions.
worked_examples.answer: Instability arose from ideological diversity, anti-Congressism as the only bond, defections, and Congress efforts to topple them; many collapsed into President's Rule.

concepts.title: The Naxalite Movement
concepts.definition: The Naxalite movement was a radical, armed peasant and communist insurgency that began in 1967 in the Naxalbari village of West Bengal's Darjeeling district. Led by Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal, it advocated a violent revolution inspired by Maoist ideology to overthrow the Indian state and redistribute land to the peasantry.
concepts.key_idea: Key aspects of the Naxalite movement: (1) origin -- the 1967 uprising in Naxalbari, West Bengal, by tribal peasants and radical communists; (2) leadership -- Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal, who broke away from the CPI(M) to form the CPI(ML) in 1969; (3) ideology -- Maoist, advocating armed guerrilla war and immediate seizure of land; (4) social base -- landless labourers, tribals and poor peasants; (5) government response -- severe police and military crackdown; (6) significance -- it exposed the failure of land reforms and the deep poverty and dispossession in rural India, and it continues in parts of central India.

solution_steps.action: Explain the ideology and social base
solution_steps.explain: Describe the Maoist ideology of armed revolution and immediate land seizure, and the social base of landless labourers, tribals and poor peasants; note the formation of the CPI(ML) in 1969.

solution_steps.action: Explain the response and significance
solution_steps.explain: Describe the severe government crackdown and the movement's significance in exposing the failure of land reforms and deep rural poverty.

worked_examples.question: What was the Naxalite movement? Explain its origins.
worked_examples.solution: The Naxalite movement was a radical, armed communist and peasant insurgency that began in 1967 in Naxalbari, a village in the Darjeeling district of West Bengal. It was led by Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal, who were radical members of the CPI(M). The uprising began when tribal peasants and landless labourers, with the support of local communist leaders, seized land from landlords. The movement was inspired by Maoist ideology and advocated a violent revolution to overthrow the Indian state. It led to the formation of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist), CPI(ML), in 1969.
worked_examples.answer: Naxalite movement = 1967 armed peasant uprising in Naxalbari, West Bengal, led by Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal, inspired by Maoism.

worked_examples.question: What were the causes of the Naxalbari uprising of 1967?
worked_examples.solution: The causes of the Naxalbari uprising included: (1) the failure of land reforms -- despite laws, landlords retained large holdings and landless peasants remained landless; (2) extreme poverty and exploitation of tribals and landless labourers in the tea gardens and farms of north Bengal; (3) the influence of Maoist ideology, especially after the Sino-Soviet split, which inspired radicals to pursue armed revolution; (4) disillusionment with the parliamentary Left (the CPI and CPI(M)) for participating in elections rather than leading revolution; (5) the immediate trigger was a dispute over land between a landlord and tribal peasants in Naxalbari.
worked_examples.answer: Causes -- failure of land reforms, rural poverty and exploitation, Maoist influence, disillusionment with the parliamentary Left, and a local land dispute.

concepts.title: The JP Movement (1974-75)
concepts.definition: The JP movement, also called the Total Revolution (Sampoorna Kranti) movement, was a mass movement launched in 1974-75 by Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) against the Congress government of Indira Gandhi. It began as a student agitation in Bihar against corruption and misgovernance and grew into a nationwide movement demanding the resignation of the Indira Gandhi government.
concepts.key_idea: Key aspects of the JP movement: (1) origin -- it began in 1974 as a student protest in Bihar against rising prices, unemployment and corruption; (2) leadership -- Jayaprakash Narayan, a respected socialist leader, was invited to lead it and gave it the call for 'Total Revolution' (sampoorna kranti) -- political, economic, social and moral; (3) the movement demanded the resignation of the Indira Gandhi government on charges of corruption; (4) it brought together opposition parties -- the Jana Sangh, socialists, Congress (O) and the CPI(M); (5) the Allahabad High Court's verdict (June 1975) invalidating Indira Gandhi's election gave the movement momentum; (6) the government responded by imposing the Emergency in June 1975.

solution_steps.action: State the origin of the JP movement
solution_steps.explain: Note that the movement began in 1974 as a student agitation in Bihar against price rise, unemployment and corruption, and that Jayaprakash Narayan was invited to lead it.

solution_steps.action: Explain the objectives and 'Total Revolution'
solution_steps.explain: Describe JP's call for 'Total Revolution' (sampoorna kranti) -- political, economic, social and moral -- and the demand for the resignation of the Indira Gandhi government on charges of corruption.

solution_steps.action: Explain the outcome and link to the Emergency
solution_steps.explain: Note that the Allahabad High Court verdict (June 1975) invalidating Indira Gandhi's election gave the movement momentum, and that the government responded by imposing the Emergency.

worked_examples.question: What was the JP movement? Explain its origins and objectives.
worked_examples.solution: The JP movement was a mass movement launched in 1974-75 by Jayaprakash Narayan against the Indira Gandhi government. It originated in Bihar as a student agitation against rising prices, unemployment and corruption. The students invited Jayaprakash Narayan, a respected socialist and freedom fighter, to lead the movement. Its objectives were: (1) to demand the resignation of the Indira Gandhi government on charges of corruption and misgovernance; (2) to bring about a 'Total Revolution' (sampoorna kranti) encompassing political, economic, social and moral change; (3) to unite the fragmented opposition against the Congress. The movement spread from Bihar to Gujarat and other parts of the country.
worked_examples.answer: JP movement = 1974-75 mass movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan, originating as a Bihar student agitation, demanding Indira Gandhi's resignation and 'Total Revolution'.

worked_examples.question: How did the JP movement contribute to the imposition of the Emergency?
worked_examples.solution: The JP movement contributed to the imposition of the Emergency in several ways: (1) it grew into a nationwide mass movement demanding the resignation of the Indira Gandhi government; (2) JP called for a nationwide satyagraha and asked the police and army not to obey unconstitutional orders; (3) on 12 June 1975, the Allahabad High Court found Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractice and invalidated her 1971 election, which strengthened the movement's demand for her resignation; (4) facing mounting pressure, Indira Gandhi advised the President to impose the Emergency on 25 June 1975, citing 'internal disturbance'. The JP movement's leaders were arrested and the movement was suppressed during the Emergency.
worked_examples.answer: The JP movement's growing pressure and the Allahabad verdict led Indira Gandhi to impose the Emergency on 25 June 1975 citing 'internal disturbance'.

concepts.title: Restoration of Democracy and the 1977 Elections
concepts.section: Restoration of Democracy and the 1977 Elections
concepts.definition: The restoration of democracy in 1977 followed the end of the Emergency. Indira Gandhi called elections for March 1977, expecting to win, but the opposition -- united as the Janata Party -- won a decisive victory. The Congress was routed, and Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress Prime Minister, marking the restoration of democratic rule.
concepts.key_idea: Key aspects of the 1977 elections and restoration: (1) Indira Gandhi ended the Emergency and called elections in March 1977; (2) the opposition parties -- Congress (O), Jana Sangh, socialists and Bharatiya Lok Dal -- merged to form the Janata Party under JP's guidance; (3) the Janata Party won 295 seats and the Congress was reduced to 154 seats; Indira Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi lost their seats; (4) Morarji Desai became PM; (5) the new government released political prisoners, restored press freedom, and repealed the Emergency provisions; (6) the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed many changes of the 42nd Amendment and strengthened safeguards against future emergencies.

solution_steps.explain: Describe how the opposition merged into the Janata Party under JP's guidance, won 295 seats, and reduced the Congress to 154 seats, with Morarji Desai becoming PM.

solution_steps.action: Explain the restoration measures
solution_steps.explain: Describe the restoration of democratic freedoms -- release of prisoners, press freedom, repeal of Emergency provisions -- and the 44th Amendment (1978) that reversed the 42nd Amendment.

worked_examples.question: How was democracy restored in India after the Emergency?
worked_examples.solution: Democracy was restored after the Emergency through the March 1977 general elections. Indira Gandhi ended the Emergency and called elections, expecting to win. However, the opposition parties -- the Congress (O), Jana Sangh, socialists and the Bharatiya Lok Dal -- merged to form the Janata Party under the guidance of Jayaprakash Narayan. The Janata Party fought the elections on the platform of restoring democracy and civil liberties. It won a decisive victory with 295 seats, while the Congress was reduced to 154 seats; both Indira Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi lost their seats. Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress Prime Minister. The new government released political prisoners, restored press freedom, and passed the 44th Amendment to reverse the 42nd Amendment.
worked_examples.answer: Democracy was restored via the 1977 elections, won by the Janata Party (295 seats); Morarji Desai became PM; freedoms were restored and the 44th Amendment reversed the 42nd.

worked_examples.question: Why did the Congress lose the 1977 elections?
worked_examples.solution: The Congress lost the 1977 elections because: (1) the excesses of the Emergency -- suspension of rights, press censorship, arrests of opposition leaders, and forced sterilisation campaigns -- had created deep public anger; (2) the opposition was united as a single Janata Party, preventing a split of the anti-Congress vote; (3) the Janata Party was supported by the JP movement's network and credibility; (4) the Congress's own organisation was weakened and many of its leaders were demoralised; (5) voters saw the election as a chance to restore democracy. The Congress was reduced to 154 seats, and both Indira Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi were defeated.
worked_examples.answer: Congress lost due to Emergency excesses, a united Janata Party, JP's support, a demoralised Congress, and a pro-democracy voter mood.

concepts.title: The Janata Party Government
concepts.definition: The Janata Party government (1977-79) was India's first non-Congress government at the Centre, led by Prime Minister Morarji Desai. Formed by a merger of four opposition parties, it came to power on the promise of restoring democracy but collapsed within two-and-a-half years due to internal differences and factionalism.
concepts.key_idea: Key aspects of the Janata Party government: (1) formation -- a merger of the Congress (O), Jana Sangh, Bharatiya Lok Dal and socialists, led by Morarji Desai as PM; (2) achievements -- restoration of democratic freedoms, release of political prisoners, the 44th Amendment reversing the 42nd, and the Mandal Commission (1979) on backward classes; (3) weaknesses -- ideological differences (especially over the 'dual membership' issue of Jana Sangh members), personal rivalries between Morarji Desai, Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram; (4) collapse -- Morarji Desai resigned in 1979, Charan Singh formed a short-lived government that fell without facing Parliament, leading to fresh elections in 1980; (5) the Janata experiment showed both the possibility and the fragility of non-Congress governments.

solution_steps.action: Describe the formation of the Janata Party government
solution_steps.explain: Note that the Janata Party was a merger of the Congress (O), Jana Sangh, Bharatiya Lok Dal and socialists, and that Morarji Desai became PM in 1977.

solution_steps.action: Explain its achievements and weaknesses
solution_steps.explain: List the achievements -- restoration of freedoms, the 44th Amendment, the Mandal Commission -- and the weaknesses -- ideological differences, the 'dual membership' controversy, and personal rivalries.

solution_steps.action: Explain the collapse and significance
solution_steps.explain: Describe how Morarji Desai resigned in 1979, Charan Singh's short-lived government fell, and fresh elections were called in 1980; note the significance of the Janata experiment for non-Congress politics.

worked_examples.question: What were the achievements of the Janata Party government?
worked_examples.solution: The Janata Party government's achievements included: (1) restoration of democratic freedoms -- release of political prisoners, restoration of press freedom and civil liberties; (2) the 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978), which reversed many authoritarian provisions of the 42nd Amendment and strengthened safeguards against future emergencies; (3) the appointment of the Mandal Commission (1979) under B.P. Mandal to investigate the conditions of backward classes; (4) efforts to decentralise power and restore the federal balance. However, its achievements were limited by its short lifespan and internal conflicts.
worked_examples.answer: Achievements -- restoration of freedoms, the 44th Amendment, the Mandal Commission, and federal decentralisation.

worked_examples.question: Why did the Janata Party government collapse in 1979?
worked_examples.solution: The Janata Party government collapsed in 1979 due to: (1) ideological differences -- the party was a merger of groups ranging from socialists to the right-wing Jana Sangh, with no common programme; (2) the 'dual membership' controversy -- some members, especially from the Jana Sangh, retained their membership of the RSS, which other partners opposed; (3) personal rivalries between Morarji Desai, Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram; (4) Charan Singh withdrew support, forcing Morarji Desai to resign in July 1979; (5) Charan Singh formed a government with Congress support but resigned within weeks without facing Parliament. Fresh elections were held in 1980, which the Congress won.
worked_examples.answer: Collapse caused by ideological differences, the dual membership controversy, personal rivalries, Charan Singh's withdrawal of support, leading to 1980 elections.

concepts.title: The Return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress (1980)
concepts.section: The Return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress (1980)
concepts.definition: The return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress to power in 1980 followed the collapse of the Janata Party government. In the 1980 Lok Sabha elections, the Congress (I) won a decisive victory, and Indira Gandhi returned as Prime Minister, marking the restoration of Congress dominance after the interlude of the Janata Party.
concepts.key_idea: Key aspects of the 1980 return: (1) context -- the collapse of the Janata Party government in 1979 due to internal divisions; (2) the 1980 elections -- the Congress (I) won 353 seats, returning to power; (3) factors for victory -- the disunity and infighting of the Janata Party, the failure of the Janata government to deliver, and Indira Gandhi's campaign emphasising stability; (4) consequences -- restoration of Congress dominance, centralisation of power, and the rise of Sanjay Gandhi's influence; (5) the period also saw the rise of regional parties and the beginning of a new phase of coalition politics in the longer term.

solution_steps.explain: Describe the factors -- Janata Party disunity and infighting, the failure of the Janata government to deliver, and Indira Gandhi's campaign emphasising stability -- that led to the Congress (I) winning 353 seats.

solution_steps.action: Explain the consequences
solution_steps.explain: Note the consequences -- restoration of Congress dominance, centralisation of power, the rise of Sanjay Gandhi's influence, and the longer-term rise of regional parties and coalition politics.

worked_examples.question: How did Indira Gandhi and the Congress return to power in 1980?
worked_examples.solution: Indira Gandhi and the Congress returned to power in 1980 after the collapse of the Janata Party government. The Janata Party, plagued by internal divisions, the dual membership controversy and personal rivalries, collapsed in 1979. Charan Singh's interim government fell without facing Parliament, and fresh elections were called for January 1980. The Congress (I) under Indira Gandhi won a decisive victory with 353 seats. Indira Gandhi's campaign emphasised the need for stability and strong government, contrasting the Janata Party's disarray. She returned as Prime Minister, restoring Congress dominance.
worked_examples.answer: The Congress (I) won 353 seats in the 1980 elections after the Janata Party's collapse, restoring Indira Gandhi as PM.

worked_examples.question: Why did the Janata Party fail to sustain the 1977 mandate?
worked_examples.solution: The Janata Party failed to sustain its 1977 mandate because: (1) it was an ideologically incoherent merger of parties ranging from socialists to the Jana Sangh, with no common programme; (2) the 'dual membership' controversy over Jana Sangh members' RSS links divided the party; (3) personal rivalries among leaders -- Morarji Desai, Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram -- prevented coherent governance; (4) the government failed to address economic problems and deliver on its promises; (5) the party spent more energy on internal disputes and targeting Indira Gandhi than on governance. These weaknesses led to its collapse in 1979 and the return of the Congress in 1980.
worked_examples.answer: The Janata Party failed due to ideological incoherence, the dual membership controversy, personal rivalries, failure to deliver, and internal disputes.

worked_examples.question_pattern: How did Indira Gandhi consolidate her position after the 1969 split?

solution_template.explain: After the 1969 split, Indira Gandhi consolidated her position by adopting a radical populist programme. She (1) nationalised major banks in 1969; (2) abolished the privy purses and privileges of former princely rulers in 1970; (3) adopted the slogan 'Garibi Hatao' (Remove Poverty); (4) presented herself as the champion of the poor against the rich and the old guard; (5) called early elections in 1971 and won a massive mandate, legitimising her leadership and the split.
